Tari 🍀🍀🍀 Sarah "Sadie" Amanda Wafer ~On this Tuesday, March 17th, 2025 I once again honor of the teachings of Saint Patrick as that relates to other real life people originally from Ireland who were immovable in their Christian faith. The Christian faith as reflected through a Catholic lens; a lens refined by that young boy of Roman descent who was captured by Irish pirates. No this is not a Hollywood script, this is real life. ❤ "Two people deeply influenced by the Catholic Church in Ireland were my Great-great grandparents, Henry and Annie. The two young people who would leave Ireland during the Great Potato Famine. Both would find their way to San Francisco where they would meet and fall in love in the city's vibrant Irish immigrant section of town. The couple married and were blessed with two children. Their eldest child, a daughter, was my Great Aunt Sarah "Sadie" Wafer. Yes, the same Great Aunt Sadie who would take my Great Grandfather to court for being a poor parent to my Grandmother. Sarah "Sadie" Amanda Wafer was a first generation American born to Irish immigrant parents in San Francisco, California. In addition to being active in San Francisco's "To Kalon Club" and "Adelphian Club," Sadie was active in numerous community service programs. She would become of the first of very few women who chose to take a "motor car," driving from San Francisco to Los Angeles, in January of 1909 to perform at the Lucchessi Benefit; a benefit for Italian earthquake survivors. Each of the five women was a musician and had more than a simple interest in helping survivors as they too had survived the Great Earthquake of 1906. Upon returning from Los Angeles, Sadie would direct much of her attention toward the San Francisco community's desire to have a permanent orchestra. In December 1911, the San Francisco Symphony gave its first concerts with Sadie as a member. Sadie would take her love for life and music with her until the end. She taught piano to untold numbers of students, including that niece she worried so much about. As was common for eldest daughters of Catholic families, Sadie never married, choosing instead to care for her parents, numerous bachelor uncles, and others without family. She passed in her beloved city of San Francisco and is buried next to her Irish mother. I am immeasurably grateful for my third great grandmother who--despite being eight months pregnant--boarded a ship with five little girls in tow. Sadie's mother was one of those little girls. For two hundred and fifty-one years, men and women have served in this honorable branch of our military to protect the liberties enjoyed by people such as you and me. A short two years later, on June 14, 1777, the Second Continental Congress concluded our new country should have an official symbolic representation. Our own John Adams stating, be it "[r]esolved, that the flag of the thirteen United States shall be thirteen stripes, alternate red and white; that the Union be thirteen stars, white on a blue field, representing a new constellation." We have served as a beacon on the hill; we continue to do so. We have been one of the most genuine and generous people ever; we continue to be so. Our best years are not behind us! Our best moment is right now in how we choose to plant the seeds for tomorrow's generations! Plant good seeds!
